description: A group of young AI engineers who love to explore the universe
summary: VeriFour - Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive, browser-based mission planning platform and GPU-accelerated 3D rover simulator that helps engineers, planners, and students evaluate where and when lunar surface sites receive sunlight and direct-to-Earth (DTE) line-of-sight from 2026 to 2030. Coupling NASA LRO LOLA South Pole laser altimetry (LDEM_75S_240M at 240 m/px) with 36,216 hourly NASA JPL Horizons (DE441 / MOON_ME) ephemeris steps, the application presents a cosmic mission-control workspace built around a Three.js 3D lunar terrain and 6-wheel rover simulator (WASD, virtual controls, and click-on-terrain autopilot waypoints with live pitch/roll slope alignment, 1x-1000x gears, 4 camera modes, and dynamic solar shadows and Earth DTE beam). Users can inspect 31 curated sites, overlay 9 Artemis III 2024 candidate polygons, compute 360-degree browser ray-marched horizons for mast heights from 0.5 m to 50 m, track 9 lunar solar eclipses, and rank polar candidates via a precomputed 250x250 grid and Web Worker scanner—verified within 0.0002 deg (Sun) and 0.0061 deg (Earth) of JPL Horizons.
details:
VeriFour – Lunar Landing Site Navigator transforms raw NASA planetary geodesy and ephemeris datasets into a NASA Eyes / Moon Trek–inspired mission-control workspace and an interactive 3D lunar rover simulator for South Pole mission planning (2026–2030). It runs entirely in the browser, with no server infrastructure.

1. KEY FEATURES

1.1 GPU-Accelerated 3D Lunar South Pole Terrain & Rover Simulator (Lunar3DViewport.tsx, roverPhysics.ts)

- Terrain and sky: Renders a 250×250 LRO LOLA South Pole terrain mesh (±150 km; selectable relief from 1× Real, a true 1:1 scale, up to 15×) with micro-regolith bump detail and 5 surface overlay layers (Regolith, Sun, Earth, Slope, Composite). The scene includes an astrometric J2000 ICRS deep-space sky (116 named bright stars, 7,200 Galactic Milky Way stars, a GLSL Milky Way dome, 7 deep-sky nebulae/galaxies and an optional Sky Guide), a glowing 3D Sun corona that casts dynamic JPL Horizons shadows (dimmed and reddened during lunar eclipses), and a sunlit crescent 3D Earth globe with a high-gain direct-to-Earth (DTE) beam. It also drapes the 9 official Artemis III (2024) candidate region boundaries and provides clickable 3D site beacons (flyTo).

- Rover: Users can deploy and drive an articulated 6-wheel rocker-bogie rover (WASD / arrow keys / virtual HUD drive pad / click-on-terrain autopilot waypoints) over a bilinearly sampled 240 m/px LRO LOLA DEM (dem_fine_240m.i16, with a seamless 1,200 m/px coarse fallback). Features include live terrain-normal pitch/roll slope alignment, selectable speed gears (1× at 4.5 m/s up to 1000× explorer warp), PSR LED headlights and 160-point 3D traverse breadcrumb trails.

- Camera modes: Rover Chase, 1st-Person Mast POV (with reticle HUD), Orbital Free Cam / Tactical, and a synchronized Command Split workspace mode.

1.2 Mission-Control Workspace, 2D Polar Map & Custom Probe (App.tsx, PolarMapCanvas.tsx)

- Five views: 3D Rover & Surface (default hero stage), Command Split, 2D Map & Sky, Compare A vs B, and Candidate Directory.

- Telemetry and notes: 4 animated SVG CircularRingGauge rings (Solar Array %, Earth DTE & window hours, 240 m Slope/Inclinometer + Rover Tilt, Composite Viability Index) and a collapsible Science & Methodology Notes accordion.

- Bottom Mission Dock (3 tabs): 14-Day Timeline & Sensitivity, 360° Horizon Sky & Panorama, and Rover Traverse Elevation Profile.

- 2D map and probe: Retains the ±150 km 2D South Pole stereographic map (250×250 illumination and Earth DTE layers plus 9 Artemis III polygons), a Global Moon view, and a click-anywhere Custom Probe Pin that is ray-marched directly in the browser.

1.3 360° Horizon Panorama, Polar Sky Dome & Hourly Mission Timeline (2026–2030)

- Horizon panorama: Displays the local 360° topographic horizon profile alongside Sun and Earth trajectories for selectable mast heights (0.5, 2.0, 10.0, 20.0 and 50.0 m for curated sites; continuous 0–50 m for custom pins), showing how raising a mast clears crater rims and shortens maximum darkness intervals.

- Timeline: Covers 2026-11-14T00:00:00Z through 2030-12-31T23:00:00Z at 1-hour cadence (36,216 steps; 9 Moon-center solar eclipses: 3 total, 6 partial). It extracts contiguous operational windows and relative solar array output (% of a perpendicular sun-tracking panel at full solar disk, vs. a horizontal deck panel).

1.4 Curated Sites, Multi-Site Comparison & Candidate Finder

- 31 curated targets: 13 South Pole candidate sites; 10 Historic & International sites (Apollo, Luna, Chang'e-4/6, Chandrayaan-3, SLIM); 6 CLPS Commercial sites (IM-1 Odysseus, IM-2 Athena, Blue Ghost); and 2 Polar Reference / PSR targets.

- Candidate Finder: Mode A filters and ranks across a precomputed 250×250 South Pole grid (1,200 m/px) plus 140 refined 5×5 (240 m/px) summit blocks (2.0 m mast), with minimum spatial-separation constraints. Mode B runs a live multi-resolution Web Worker (scanAroundWorker) around any selected coordinate.

2. HOW WE USED NASA DATA: FROM EDA TO THE APP

2.1 Explore first (EDA, before building)

We ran an exploratory data analysis of the two core NASA datasets before writing any app code (the notebooks stay local and are not published in the repository).

- JPL Horizons: Hourly Sun/Earth sub-points on the Moon (MOON_ME frame), with no gaps or duplicates. Vector geometry on this single table reproduces Horizons' own per-site Az/El to ≤ 0.0002° (Sun) and ≤ 0.006° (Earth), so the app never needs to call Horizons at runtime.

- LRO LOLA LDEM_75S_240M: A 3812×3812 int16 elevation grid (−7.76 km to +7.02 km, no empty pixels). Ray-marching the horizon over this DEM showed that terrain decides everything:

- Connecting Ridge receives about 91% Sun with terrain, but only about 54% on a smooth sphere.

- The Shackleton floor receives 0% Sun and 0% Earth.

- Moving about 170 m changed Sun time by 13 percentage points.

- Landing date alone swings "Sun + Earth" time from 0% to 100%.

2.2 What the EDA changed in the design

- Finding: One ephemeris table is enough for any location.

-> Decision: Zero-backend app with a precomputed ephemeris.json.

- Finding: Terrain dominates; position and date are highly sensitive.

-> Decision: Show Sun % and Earth % together, with a 360° horizon panorama, a multi-year timeline and A/B comparison.

- Finding: The 240 m DEM smooths near-field terrain.

-> Decision: State limits openly and report n/a outside 75°S–90°S.

2.3 Build

The offline pipeline (scripts/) converts raw NASA files into compact browser assets (int16 DEM grids and JSON). The React app ray-marches these grids in the browser to compute illumination, Earth visibility and the viability score, and uses the same DEM and Horizons Sun positions to render the 3D terrain, lighting and rover.

2.4 Verify

Results are checked against Horizons topocentric tables and the literature (see Section 3).

3. METHOD & SCIENTIFIC VALIDATION

- Spherical horizon ray-marching: For each target, 360 azimuth rays (1° spacing) march along exact lunar great circles (R0 = 1,737.4 km) across 480 log-spaced steps from 120 m to 200 km. They sample the 240 m/px fine LOLA DEM inside ±150 km and the 1,200 m/px 5×5 block-max LOLA DEM out to 75°S.

- Finite solar disk & joint visibility: The app distinguishes sun_time_pct (any part of the 0.266° solar disk above the horizon) from sun_visible_pct (mean visible solar-disk fraction), and strictly enforces both_visible_pct ≤ min(sun_time_pct, earth_visible_pct).

- JPL Horizons DE441 / MOON_ME validation: Checked across 6 lunar sites over 36,216 hours, with a maximum angular error of 0.000198° (Sun) and 0.006016° (Earth).

- Literature cross-check: Benchmarked in-app (About & Data modal) against Mazarico et al. (2011), De Rosa et al. (2012), Gläser et al. (2014, 2018), Barker et al. (2021, 2023), and NASA PDS LOLA AVGVISIB maps.

4. BENEFITS & KNOWN LIMITATIONS

Benefits: VeriFour runs 100% client-side in standard web browsers, with zero server infrastructure and no live API latency. This makes authentic NASA LOLA and JPL Horizons mission analysis and 3D lunar rover traversal accessible to researchers, students and hackathon judges worldwide.

Limitations:

- LDEM_75S_240M (240 m/px) and the 250×250 3D mesh provide exploratory, decision-support fidelity. They do not resolve meter-scale boulders, lander footpad slopes or regolith terramechanics.

- The Composite Viability Score is a transparent, team-defined heuristic, not an engineering flight certification.

- Sites north of 75°S report n/a for local DEM terrain statistics and use smooth-sphere horizon-dip geometry.

5. TOOLS, LANGUAGES & STACK

- Frontend (webapp/): React 18.3, TypeScript 5.6, Three.js 0.187 (WebGL 3D), Vite 6, Tailwind CSS v4, HTML5 Canvas 2D & SVG, Web Workers, Lucide Icons, Vitest (67 active unit/integration tests + 34 todo scaffolds).

- Offline data pipeline (scripts/): Python 3.13+, NumPy, Pandas, SciPy, Requests, unittest/pytest (10 pipeline invariant tests).
